lesson.title: Building Reactions You Can't Run: Solving with Hess's Law
lesson.summary: Hess's law becomes a calculation tool once you learn the systematic procedure: manipulate a set of known equations, by reversing and scaling them, until they add up to your target equation, then apply the same manipulations to their delta H values.
lesson.body:
Knowing that enthalpy is path independent, as established in the Hess's law chapter, is only useful once you can act on it. The standard procedure for a Hess's law calculation is this: write down the target equation whose delta H you want, then look at each given equation and figure out what has to happen to it, does it need to be reversed, does it need to be multiplied by some factor, so that when all the given equations are added together, everything except the target's reactants and products cancels out. Whatever you do to an equation, you do the identical thing to its delta H: reversing an equation flips the sign of delta H, and scaling an equation by a factor multiplies delta H by that same factor. Once the equations sum correctly, adding the manipulated delta H values gives the target's enthalpy of reaction, which is exactly the enthalpy-of-reaction quantity from two chapters back, just obtained indirectly.

Let's work a real three-equation example: finding the enthalpy of formation of methane, C(s) + 2 H2(g) -> CH4(g), using three reactions whose enthalpies are well established. Given: (1) C(s) + O2(g) -> CO2(g), delta H1 = -393.5 kJ. (2) H2(g) + 1/2 O2(g) -> H2O(l), delta H2 = -285.8 kJ. (3) CH4(g) + 2 O2(g) -> CO2(g) + 2 H2O(l), delta H3 = -890.4 kJ.

Look at the target: it needs C(s) and 2 H2(g) as reactants and CH4(g) as the only product, with no O2, CO2, or H2O appearing at all. Equation (1) already has C(s) on the reactant side, so use it as is. The target needs 2 H2(g), so double equation (2): 2 H2(g) + O2(g) -> 2 H2O(l), delta H = 2 x (-285.8 kJ) = -571.6 kJ. CH4 needs to end up as a product, but in equation (3) it is a reactant, so reverse equation (3): CO2(g) + 2 H2O(l) -> CH4(g) + 2 O2(g), delta H = +890.4 kJ.

Now add all three manipulated equations. Left sides: C(s) + O2(g) + 2 H2(g) + O2(g) + CO2(g) + 2 H2O(l). Right sides: CO2(g) + 2 H2O(l) + CH4(g) + 2 O2(g). The CO2(g) cancels (appears on both sides), the 2 H2O(l) cancels, and the oxygen tallies to 2 O2(g) on each side and cancels too. What remains is exactly the target: C(s) + 2 H2(g) -> CH4(g). Summing the enthalpies with their manipulations applied: -393.5 kJ + (-571.6 kJ) + (+890.4 kJ). Adding step by step: -393.5 + (-571.6) = -965.1, then -965.1 + 890.4 = -74.7 kJ. So the enthalpy of formation of methane comes out to about -74.7 kJ/mol, which lines up well with the commonly tabulated experimental value near -74.8 kJ/mol.

Notice what made this work: every manipulation, doubling equation (2), reversing equation (3), was chosen deliberately so that the unwanted species (O2, CO2, H2O) would cancel when the equations were added, leaving only the target's reactants and products. That cancellation check is the real skill in these problems: before you even add the enthalpies, verify on paper that the chemical equations actually sum to your target. If they do not cancel cleanly, the calculation is wrong no matter how carefully you added the numbers.
